Delta tracking efficiency depends on the tightness of the majorant $\sigma_m$ [S1].

The evidence explicitly defines the majorant $σ_m$ as the upper bound of the extinction coefficient $σ_t$. It describes the 'Delta tracking' (or Woodcock tracking) algorithm which relies on sampling distances based on the homogenized transmittance $τ_m = exp(-σ_m t)$. The efficiency of this algorithm is inherently dependent on the tightness of $σ_m$ because a tighter majorant (closer to the actual $σ_t$) results in a lower probability of hitting 'fake particles' (which require no scattering but consume a sample), thus reducing the number of bounces needed to reach a real interaction or the surface. While the text doesn't use the exact phrase 'efficiency depends on tightness', the mechanism described (sampling from $σ_m$ to handle heterogeneous media) is the standard definition of why the majorant's tightness matters for delta tracking performance. Every factual component (majorant definition, delta tracking mechanism, dependence on sampling from majorant) is present and consistent with the claim.

# Hit real particle: Scatter [S1]

The evidence explicitly describes the 'Null-scattering' technique (also known as Delta tracking or Woodcock tracking). It details how heterogeneous media are converted into homogeneous media using 'fake particles' that do not scatter light. It further explains the sampling process where, upon sampling a distance, one of three outcomes occurs: hitting a surface, hitting a 'real particle' (which causes scattering), or hitting a 'fake particle' (which continues the ray in a straight line). The claim '# Hit real particle: Scatter [S1]' accurately summarizes the event corresponding to hitting a real particle in this algorithm as described in the source.
